trial_name: EMERGE — Emergency vs Delayed Coronary Angiogram in Survivors of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (2022)
citation: Hauw-Berlemont C, Lamhaut L, Diehl JL, et al; EMERGE Trial Investigators. Emergency vs delayed coronary angiogram in survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: results of the randomized, multicentric EMERGE trial. JAMA Cardiol. 2022;7(7):700-707.
one_liner: In OHCA survivors without ST-segment elevation, routine emergency coronary angiography did not improve 180-day neurologically intact survival compared with a delayed strategy (48-96 hours).

pico.population: Adult survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with sustained ROSC, no ST-segment elevation, no obvious non-cardiac cause
pico.intervention: Emergency coronary angiography strategy (immediate transfer to cath lab, PCI if culprit lesion)
pico.comparison: Delayed coronary angiography strategy (planned at 48–96 hours, urgent angiography allowed if clinically indicated)
pico.outcome: 180-day survival free of major neurological sequelae (CPC 1–2)

background.existing_knowledge: OHCA survivors without ST-elevation can have acute coronary culprit lesions, and post-ROSC ECG has imperfect sensitivity. Observational data and early cardiac arrest centre pathways supported routine early angiography as potentially time-critical.
background.knowledge_gap: Equipoise persisted regarding whether a routine 'go-to-cath-lab' strategy improves patient-centred outcomes vs a selective or delayed approach, given competing post-arrest ICU priorities.
background.hypothesis: Emergency CAG strategy would be superior to delayed CAG (48–96 h) for 180-day neurologically intact survival.

methods.design: Investigator-initiated, multicentre, open-label, randomised, parallel-group, superiority trial
methods.setting: France; centres with ICU and 24/7 interventional cardiology; enrolment June/2018–?/2022 (stopped early)

inclusion: Adults ≥18 years with out-of-hospital sudden cardiac arrest and sustained ROSC
No obvious non-cardiac cause identified at presentation
No ischaemic ST-segment elevation on post-ROSC ECG (LBBB not treated as STEMI equivalent)
Admitted to centre with ICU and 24/7 interventional cardiology
exclusion: Major comorbidity with life expectancy <1 year

methods.intervention: Emergency coronary angiography: immediate transfer to cath lab as soon as feasible; PCI if culprit lesion identified.
methods.comparison: Delayed coronary angiography planned for 48–96 hours after ICU admission; urgent angiography before planned window permitted if clinically indicated.
methods.blinding: Open-label for clinicians; primary endpoint assessed by an independent physician masked to allocation.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 970 to detect 10% absolute improvement (36%→46%) with 80% power, two-sided α=0.05, allowing 30% crossover and 10% loss to follow-up. Stopped early after 338 randomised; 279 analysed.
methods.primary_outcome: 180-day survival free of major neurological sequelae (CPC 1–2)
methods.follow_up: 180 days (neurological outcome also at ICU discharge and 90 days)

headline_bullets: Emergency CAG did not improve 180-day neurologically intact survival: 34.1% vs 30.7% (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65–1.15, P=0.32).
Large separation in angiography timing (median 2h vs 65.5h from arrest) but no patient-centred outcome benefit.
Early stopping substantially reduced statistical power; wide CIs do not exclude clinically important effects.

outcomes_table.outcome: 180-day survival free of major neurological sequelae (CPC 1–2)
outcomes_table.note: Time-to-event analysis; major neurological sequelae = CPC 3–5
Delayed group: 23/74 (31.1%) urgent angiography before planned window

outcomes_table.outcome: Time from OHCA to angiography, median (IQR), hours

outcomes_table.note: Competing pathway for outcome; no between-group difference

subgroup_table.subgroup: Pre-specified prognostic strata: Group 1 (age<75, shockable, no-flow<5, low-flow<20, epi<1 mg)

safety: Shock during first 48 hours: 38.8% vs 39.8% (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.76–1.39)
VT/VF during first 48 hours: 7.1% vs 3.6% (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.18–1.46)
Withdrawal of life-sustaining care: 39.7% vs 47.1% (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.91–1.55)

domains.notes: Centralised web-based 1:1, variable blocks, stratified by prognostic stratum. Randomisation early (prehospital or within 1h). Allocation concealed.
Open-label; co-interventions (e.g., haemodynamic support, neuroprognostication) could be influenced. Primary outcome assessed by masked physician.

338 randomised, 59 (17.5%) excluded post-randomisation (37 lack of consent, 16 ineligible, 6 other). 279 analysed = modified ITT. Deferred consent with post-randomisation exclusion may introduce selection bias.
Emergency group: angiography 89.4%; delayed: only 53.6% had angiography, 31.1% of those early/urgent (within 14.7h). PCI among those catheterised 30.2% vs 23.0%.
Broadly similar: age 65.4 vs 63.9, male 73.1% vs 66.7%, non-shockable rhythm 65.2% vs 69.9%, GCS median 3 in both, TTM 52% vs 53.7%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate: randomisation and separation in timing were strong, but early stopping, substantial post-randomisation exclusions, and control group non-adherence reduce precision and raise residual bias.

domains.notes: Pragmatic OHCA cohort without ST-elevation, majority non-shockable rhythms, reflecting real-world case-mix. Enrolled only in centres with 24/7 cath lab and ICU – may select for higher-resource systems.

Applicable to OHCA survivors without ST-elevation or obvious non-cardiac cause. Results support an ICU-first, selective invasive strategy where urgent angiography is available. Cautious extrapolation to systems with different neuroprognostication or withdrawal-of-care practices.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate: population is clinically representative, but generalisability is strongest in resource-rich systems with structured regional pathways.

strengths: Randomised design addressing a high-impact systems-of-care question
Clinically meaningful primary outcome (neurologically intact survival at 180 days)
Early randomisation (prehospital/early hospital) testing real-world pathway decision
Substantial achieved separation in angiography timing (median 2h vs 65.5h)
limitations: Early stopping for funding/recruitment shortfall, 279 of planned 970 → underpowered, wide CIs
Post-randomisation exclusions for consent/eligibility (17.5%), deviating from strict ITT
Protocol non-adherence in delayed group: only 53.6% underwent angiography, 23 patients urgent early angiography
High competing risk of neurological death limiting proportion who can benefit from revascularisation

critical_appraisal.summary: EMERGE is a moderate-quality RCT that found no benefit of routine emergency angiography on neurologically intact survival, but early stopping, protocol deviations, and wide confidence intervals limit definitive conclusions; in context of other trials, supports a selective invasive strategy.
weaknesses: Control group contamination and low angiography rate

sections.authors_conclusion: A routine emergency angiography strategy did not improve neurologically intact survival compared with a delayed strategy. These data support an ICU-first, selective invasive strategy, with urgent angiography reserved for evolving clinical indications.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: In OHCA survivors without ST-elevation, routine immediate angiography is not superior to a delayed (48-96h) strategy; practice should be ICU-first with selective/urgent angiography when clinically indicated.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults after OHCA without ST-elevation, no obvious non-cardiac cause, managed in centres with cath-lab capability and ICU.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: This does not apply to patients with STEMI or those with clear non-cardiac aetiologies, nor does it preclude urgent angiography for haemodynamic instability or recurrent ischaemia.
implementation_caveats: Ensure capacity for urgent angiography within hours if clinically indicated
Post-arrest care bundles and neuroprognostication may influence outcomes independent of revascularisation
Systems should develop clear criteria for early vs delayed catheterisation

controversies.notes: Stopping far short of planned sample size leaves wide confidence intervals that cannot exclude clinically important benefit or harm.
Excluding 59 participants after allocation (mainly lack of consent) may introduce selection bias if exclusions are associated with prognosis or pathway.
Delayed strategy included no angiography (often early death) and urgent early angiography in 23 patients, complicating attribution to timing alone.
Historic registry and consensus support for early angiography conflicts with EMERGE and other RCTs; nearly half of catheterised patients had no significant coronary disease.

context_related_trials.relation: Also found no benefit of immediate vs delayed angiography in OHCA without ST-elevation, with largely neutral results.
Similar neutral findings for immediate angiography in post-cardiac arrest without STEMI.
Large randomised trial confirming no benefit of immediate angiography vs delayed/selective strategy in the same population.

unresolved_questions: How to better select patients with potentially reversible coronary occlusion (biomarkers, imaging, refined ECG criteria)?
Impact of withdrawal-of-care practices on outcome assessment in open-label trials?
Systems-level evaluation of pathways incorporating patient-centred outcomes and competing risks?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In comatose OHCA survivors without ST-elevation, don't rush to the cath lab – an ICU-first selective strategy is just as good.
